video_title: The Bull Market May Be Over: Hedge Funds Are Already Selling | Kevin Muir
gist: Kevin Muir (The Macro Tourist) argues the secular bull market is over: pod-shop degrossing and short-gamma positioning hide fragility beneath a calm S&P 500, AI is an earnings bubble exposed by Nvidia's vendor financing, and an overly hawkish Fed tightening into an oil shock risks recession. He favors cash, front-end bonds and international stocks, stays long-term bullish on gold (PBoC buying) though wary near term, and sees an SPR-refill floor under oil.

themes.theme: Pod-shop degrossing and hidden index fragility

insights.claim: Kevin Muir says the current hedge-fund/pod-shop pain is about the worst it has been, rivaling the 2007 quant quake, with longs falling and shorts squeezing simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Factor/crowding unwinds can inflict large losses even while the index barely moves; monitor long-short factor baskets, not just the S&P.
insights.quote: it's about the worst it's been. It's like this is in essence kind of rivaling the quant quake of 2007

insights.claim: Goldman Sachs' AI winners-versus-losers basket hit all-time highs roughly a month to a month and a half ago and is now down about 40%.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Signals a violent reversal in the crowded AI long; use the basket as a gauge of the unwind.
insights.quote: It's like AI winners versus losers. That trade like a month ago or a month and a half ago was, you know, hitting all-time highs and now it's down off 40%.

insights.claim: Consumer staples (XLP) and Costco are hitting new highs not on fundamentals but because pod shops that funded AI longs by shorting staples are being forced to cover.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Staples strength may be a short-covering artifact that fades once degrossing ends; be wary of chasing it.
insights.quote: XLP is running to new highs. Like it's just it's it's it's running like it stole something.

insights.claim: Muir argues professional degrossing is flattering the S&P 500 (only ~6-7% off highs) because short-covering rallies offset falling longs; once the forced chasing wears off, he expects the whole index to roll over.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Index-level calm masks internal stress; retail 401k holders face more downside than headline levels imply.
insights.quote: The whole index will roll over.

insights.claim: Dispersion between rising staples and falling AI stocks compresses index-level volatility, lulling investors into taking more risk; if correlation normalizes, volatility jumps and vol-targeting and market-maker hedging force more selling.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Watch implied correlation; a correlation spike is the mechanism that converts dispersion into an index-level selloff.

insights.claim: Citing Vincent Delawir, Muir notes that applying normal correlation to current single-stock implied volatilities would put the VIX at 35-40 rather than 15-20.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: VIX understates latent risk; cheap index vol may be mispriced relative to single-name vol.
insights.quote: then the VIX wouldn't be 15 or 20, it would be 35 or 40

themes.theme: AI as an earnings bubble, not a price bubble

insights.claim: Muir contends the market is in an earnings bubble rather than a price bubble: hyperscaler capex (e.g. Microsoft borrowing $100B for data centers split among GPUs, buildings and cooling) is booked immediately as revenue by suppliers while the buyer amortizes the cost over about seven years, inflating aggregate S&P earnings.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: 'Cheap' P/Es on AI names may rest on unsustainable earnings; stress-test valuations against a capex slowdown.
insights.quote: I contend that we've been in an earnings bubble, not a price bubble.

insights.claim: The 'one big beautiful bill' allowing full first-year expensing pulls tax benefits forward, encouraging more capex now while leaving future periods with amortization losses that cannot be deducted.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Tax-driven pull-forward of AI capex raises the risk of a later earnings and spending air pocket.

insights.claim: Muir says he is not an AI skeptic but a skeptic of AI security prices, noting nine of the top ten US stocks are technology names closely tied to the AI bubble, distorting the indexes.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Index investors are heavily concentrated in one theme; check true look-through tech exposure.
insights.quote: I'm a skeptic on the price of the securities in there

insights.claim: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's recent scandal and vendor financing undercut the infinite-GPU-demand story: echoing Tracy Alloway, Muir asks why anyone with infinite demand would need to take such risks or lend customers money to buy product.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Treat vendor financing as a late-cycle demand red flag for the AI hardware complex.
insights.quote: If there was infinite demand for GPUs, which has been the story for the past year, year and a half or whatever it is that this AI bull market has been there, if there was infinite demand, why would he risk this?

insights.claim: Muir draws a direct parallel between Nvidia's vendor financing and Nortel and Lucent in the dot-com bubble, predicting AI earnings will prove unrealistic and fall faster than expected once data-center building slows.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Dot-com telecom-equipment playbook suggests sharp earnings reversals for AI suppliers when capex decelerates.
insights.quote: we're going to be shocked at how far how fast they come down

insights.claim: Going into this earnings season, analysts raised rather than lowered forecasts (no 'guide down to beat'), baking in near-unprecedented growth that made AI stocks almost an easy short.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: When estimates rise into prints, the bar is too high; beats may not be enough.
insights.quote: it just ended up being kind of almost an easy short

insights.claim: Muir rejects the narrative that the Democrats winning Congress caused the AI selloff, noting the market rose the day of the result and that until recently widening hyperscaler option-adjusted spreads were treated as bullish for AI stocks; prices make the news.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Don't anchor on the political narrative; the driver is positioning and demand doubts.
insights.quote: everyone thinks news makes the prices but often prices make the news

themes.theme: Secular bear market and the Nifty Fifty analogy

insights.claim: Muir believes the secular bull market ended with the AI-led Nasdaq push to new highs last month and that a secular bear market is beginning as stocks reprice to more appropriate valuations.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Long-horizon buy-and-hold in US mega-caps may face years of poor real returns.
insights.quote: I happen to be much more in the camp that the secular bull is over.

insights.claim: Today resembles the Nifty Fifty era, when beloved brand stocks like Xerox, RCA and McDonald's traded at immense multiples and delivered roughly zero returns over the next 20 years despite not losing money.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Quality blue chips bought at euphoric multiples can still mean decades of dead money.
insights.quote: when you looked at the return of that stock over the next 20 years it was zero

insights.claim: A stock must beat what is already priced in, not merely do well; buying names like AMD requires an edge over market expectations. Muir cites Jim Grant: a good investment is one everyone agrees with later.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Assess expectations embedded in prices rather than business quality alone.
insights.quote: it's not enough that your stock does well. It needs to do better than what's expected

insights.claim: Cap-weighted products like QQQ are treated as diversified, yet a Canadian adviser replicating the Nasdaq 100 stock by stock would breach concentration limits for too much tech.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: ETF wrappers disguise concentration risk; audit overlapping tech exposure across funds.

insights.claim: During the past month's selloff professionals monetized their put hedges and then got long, citing year-end seasonality, the belief that Anthropic and the authorities 'won't let it go down', and elevated volatility.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: An unhedged, long-positioned professional community removes a cushion for the next leg down.

insights.claim: Muir still assigns roughly a 70% chance that the market grinds higher, but argues the downside tail is now much fatter: a drop would be 10-20% rather than 5%, so the payoff profile has deteriorated.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Buying dips remains the base case but consider cheap tail protection given skewed downside.
insights.quote: if we go down five, I don't think we're going to go down just five. >> It's going to be 10, 20, whatever it is.

insights.claim: Market makers are in a short-gamma position, forcing them to sell into declines and buy into rallies, which would accelerate any rollover.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Dealer positioning makes downside moves nonlinear; watch gamma levels for crash risk.

themes.theme: Fed policy error, bonds and cash

insights.claim: Muir expects inflation to surprise to the downside cyclically because the economy rolls over, even though he believes a secular era of higher inflation has begun, with the Fed missing its target for 68 consecutive months.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Position for a cyclical disinflation/recession inside a secular inflation regime; be nimble.
insights.quote: The Federal Reserve has not met their target for the past 68 months.

insights.claim: The Fed has turned more hawkish, putting a 50bp hike on the table for the upcoming FOMC, and Muir expects it to tighten into the oil supply shock from the war and cause a recession: a classic Fed error.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Hawkish Fed is bad for stocks and the economy but bullish for long-duration bonds on a policy-error view.
insights.quote: It's going to tighten into a supply ch shock, which is the the shock of the of the war with the oil, and it's going to throw us into a recession.

insights.claim: Muir has started buying bonds for the first time in this cycle, including two-year notes and more complex trades betting on a lower forward curve, because an overly hawkish Fed is good for the long end.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Front-end and forward-curve receivers are his preferred expression of a Fed-induced slowdown.
insights.quote: I bought some two years and I I put some complicated more complicated trades on to bet on forward curve being lower

insights.claim: Long bonds are less reliable as a hedge than in the past because of large deficits: in a slowdown the Fed may cut but the yield curve could steepen and term premium explode, so Muir prefers front-end exposure or cash.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Favor short duration over long duration as a recession hedge.
insights.quote: Term premium might explode.

insights.claim: Cash is the 'hard trade' now: Warren Buffett had a record cash pile before retiring as Berkshire chairman, and cash provides optionality to buy cheap stocks when others are in trouble, though it loses purchasing power over the long run.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Raise cash as dry powder despite FOMO; accept long-run inflation drag for near-term optionality.
insights.quote: what is the hard trade right now? What is it the the most difficult to do? And one of those answers is cash.

insights.claim: To avoid owning what everyone else owns (US tech, the most crowded trade), Muir recommends diversifying internationally, noting Japan's index is up about twice as much as the US year to date and the US has not outperformed over the past year and a half.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Rotate some equity exposure to Japan/Europe to reduce crowding risk.

themes.theme: Gold: long-term PBoC bid vs short-term liquidity drain

insights.claim: Muir's long-term gold bull case rests on the People's Bank of China diversifying into gold for years or decades after the West froze Russia's reserves in 2022, buying slowly to avoid pushing the price up.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Structural central-bank bid supports gold over the long run.
insights.quote: you have to diversify into something that is truly nobody's liability, and that's gold

insights.claim: Gold is struggling short term because real rates are rising with a hawkish Fed, the US dollar is bid, and liquidity appears to be draining (SOFR traded outside the Fed's bands at end-October), with Western investors overwhelming PBoC buying.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Expect gold weakness to persist until the Fed pivots dovish.

insights.claim: Gold held 4,000/3,950, broke below, then failed to reclaim the range convincingly; Muir has no short-term view and warns the initial move in gold during a financial accident might be lower.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Key technical levels: 3,950-4,000; a liquidity event could hit gold first before it rallies.
insights.quote: one of the things I worry about is the initial move in gold might be lower

insights.claim: Once hawkish Fed talk triggers a nonlinear equity break (as in Powell's 2018 'long way from neutral'), the Fed will be forced to pivot and gold should lead the next move higher; that is the time to buy.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Wait for the Fed pivot trigger to add gold aggressively.
insights.quote: everyone will rush into gold and it will lead the way out of the next, you know, move higher

themes.theme: Oil floor from SPR depletion and restocking

insights.claim: Oil did not spike to $200 after the Strait of Hormuz closed in the Iran war because US SPR releases and China's stockpiles were far larger than assumed; the US SPR is now nearly empty.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: The buffer that capped oil is exhausted, raising upside risk on future supply shocks.

insights.claim: Muir doubts oil returns to $40-50 even in a slowdown because countries must refill strategic reserves; India has already announced doubling its SPR and will be a buyer for months to years.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Restocking demand puts a floor under crude; be cautious being structurally short oil.
insights.quote: I'm not as is hopeful that oil is ever going back to 40 bucks

insights.claim: A more unstable world and US allies boosting fiscal spending because Trump says they can't rely on the US both argue for commodity stockpiling and secular inflation; any cyclical disinflation will be met with easy policy and a quick chase back into real assets.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Stay nimble: use cyclical dips to rebuild real-asset exposure.
